content_html:
This calculator is for a mortgage you already have. Instead of starting from the price of a home, it starts from the balance on your latest statement and answers two questions: how much sooner will extra payments clear the loan, and how much would you need to pay to be done by a particular year?

How to use this calculator

  1. Remaining loan balance: the unpaid principal shown on your mortgage statement or online account.
  2. Interest rate: your current note rate.
  3. Remaining term or monthly payment: enter whichever you know. If you choose the payment, use principal and interest only, without escrow for taxes and insurance.
  4. Your payoff plan: any mix of a fixed extra amount each month, a larger amount once a year (for example from a tax refund or bonus) and a lump sum paid now.
  5. Target: optional. Enter a number of years to see the monthly payment that clears the loan by then.

How the payoff is calculated

If you enter the remaining term, the regular payment comes from the standard formula P = B × i / (1 − (1 + i)−n), where B is the balance, i is the yearly rate divided by 12 and n is the months left. The calculator then runs the loan month by month twice: once with only the regular payment and once with your extra money added to principal. The difference in the number of payments and in total interest is your saving. For a target date, it solves the same formula for the number of months you choose and subtracts your current payment.

A worked example

Say you owe $250,000 at 6.5% with 25 years left. Your principal and interest payment is $1,688.02, and if you simply keep paying it you will pay $256,405.37 more in interest.

PlanTime to payoffInterest left to pay
Regular payments25 years$256,405.37
$200 extra every month19 years 6 months$191,477.49
$489.76 extra every month15 years$141,997.14

The extra $200 a month adds up to $46,600 of extra principal and saves $64,927.88 in interest, cutting 5 years and 6 months from the loan. Entering a 15-year target shows that $489.76 a month on top of the regular payment would clear the balance in exactly 15 years.

Before you prepay

  • Check for a prepayment penalty. Federal rules in place since 2014 limit prepayment penalties on most mortgages to the first three years, but read your note to be sure.
  • Mark extra money as principal. Otherwise a servicer may hold it as an early payment rather than reducing the balance.
  • Keep an emergency fund. Money paid into your home is hard to get back out without selling or borrowing against it.
  • Compare with other uses. Paying down a 6.5% mortgage is like earning a guaranteed 6.5% before tax. High-interest debt usually deserves the money first, and an employer retirement match is often worth more.
  • Consider refinancing too. Moving to a shorter term at a lower rate can cut interest further, though closing costs apply.

Limits of this estimate

Results cover principal and interest only and assume a fixed rate with no missed payments. Dates assume your next payment is due next month. For the exact amount to close the loan on a given day, request a payoff statement from your servicer, since interest accrues daily up to the payoff date.

faq.question: Does paying extra lower my monthly payment?
faq.answer: Not on a standard fixed-rate mortgage. The required payment stays the same and the loan simply ends sooner. Some lenders will recast the loan after a large lump sum, lowering the payment for the remaining term, usually for a small fee.

faq.question: Is it better to pay extra monthly or once a year?
faq.answer: Spreading the same total across monthly payments saves slightly more, because each dollar starts reducing interest sooner. The difference is modest, so choose the pattern that fits your budget and that you will stick to.

faq.question: What is a mortgage payoff statement?
faq.answer: It is a document from your servicer showing the exact amount needed to close the loan by a specific date, including interest up to that day and any fees. You need one to pay off the loan or to sell or refinance.

faq.question: Will paying off my mortgage early affect my credit score?
faq.answer: Closing an installment loan can cause a small, usually temporary change in your score because it alters your mix of accounts. The long-term effect of having less debt is generally positive.

faq.question: Should I pay off my mortgage or invest the money?
faq.answer: It depends on your rate, taxes, other debts and how much risk you are comfortable with. Prepaying gives a certain return equal to your mortgage rate, while investing may earn more or less. Many people do some of each.
